chapters.title: Map a Habit's Three Parts Before You Try to Break It
chapters.hook: Tonight you'll just be stronger, you tell yourself, standing at the open fridge for the third night in a row.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think breaking a bad habit takes more willpower and wanting it more. Actually, you need to see the habit's three parts first, because once a habit forms, it runs without the thinking part of your brain fully taking part.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before you try to change a habit, write down its cue, its routine and its reward.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one habit you want to change and write its cue, routine and reward on a sticky note before dinner tonight.

memorableLines.text: A habit you can name in three parts is a habit you can change.

Trying harder fails because once a habit forms, the thinking part of your brain stops fully taking part. Charles Duhigg, a New York Times reporter, says every habit is a loop with three parts. A cue, like walking in the door, tells your brain which habit to run. The routine is the action itself. The reward tells your brain the loop is worth keeping. At MIT, rats learning a maze for chocolate showed less and less brain activity as the run became a habit. Eugene Pauly lost his memory to a brain infection and could not say where he lived. Yet he learned to walk around his block each day and come home. The scientist Larry Squire studied him and showed that habits live apart from memory.

So Kenji writes three lines on an envelope. Cue: home and tired at six. Routine: couch and phone. Reward: switching off from work. Now he faces a loop he can see, not a weakness. Write down a habit's trigger, action and payoff before you fight it, and you will know what to change.

breakdown.fullRead:
Kenji gets home at six, drops his keys in the bowl and sinks onto the couch with his phone. The run he planned is gone again, the third evening this week, and his first 10K race is a month away. Tonight he deletes the app and swears he will try harder. It feels like the obvious fix. His phone holds plenty of other apps, and by seven his thumb has found one.

Kenji blames himself. He decides he just doesn't want the run badly enough, so the answer must be to want it more. Most people treat a bad habit the same way, as a contest of will they keep losing. But willpower works on choices, and by six o'clock there is hardly a choice left to make. Something else has already decided.

Charles Duhigg, a New York Times reporter, explains what that something is. The brain is always looking for ways to save effort. When it repeats a chain of actions often enough, it turns them into one automatic routine. Scientists call this chunking. It happens in the basal ganglia, an old part buried deep in the brain. Once a habit forms, the thinking part of the brain stops fully taking part in the decision. That frees it for other work. It also means the habit runs on its own, unless you deliberately fight it or find a new routine.

Duhigg calls the pattern a habit loop, and it has three parts. First comes a cue, the trigger that tells your brain to go on autopilot and which habit to run. Walking in the door at six is a cue. Next comes the routine, the behavior itself, like the couch and the scrolling. Last comes the reward, the payoff that tells your brain this loop is worth keeping. For Kenji, that might be the feeling of switching off after a long day. Run the loop enough times, and it starts before you notice.

Scientists at MIT watched this happen in rats. Each rat learned a maze with a piece of chocolate at one end. At first its brain was busy the whole way, as if it were working out every step. After many runs, the rat raced to the chocolate, and its brain activity dropped and kept dropping. What work remained bunched up at the start of the run and at the end, when the chocolate came. In between, the brain went quiet. The routine in the middle had become automatic.

The strongest proof came from a man named Eugene Pauly. A brain infection destroyed much of his memory, and he could not hold on to anything new for long. Asked where his kitchen was, he had no idea. Yet when he got hungry, he stood up and walked straight to it. Over time he learned to walk around his block each day and come back home, though he could not say where he lived. Larry Squire, a memory scientist, studied him closely and showed that habits live apart from memory. If a habit can run in a man who remembers almost nothing, it can run right past your good intentions.

That is why Duhigg's first step is to see the loop, not to grit your teeth. Pick one habit you want to change this week and write down its three parts. To find the cue, notice what happens just before the habit starts. Name the routine plainly. For the reward, ask what you get out of it, even if part of you hates the habit. A loop that keeps running is paying you something. Until you can name all three, you are fighting something you cannot see.

Kenji takes an envelope from the counter and writes three lines. Cue: home and tired at six. Routine: couch and phone. Reward: switching off from work after a long day. Seen this way, the evening is not a test of character he keeps failing. It is a loop with a trigger and a payoff, and he can plan around both. Write down a habit's trigger, action and payoff before you fight it, and you will know what to change.

examples.title: Twenty minutes lost after every no
examples.scenario: Ines sells office software by phone. Whenever a call ends in a flat no, she opens a celebrity news site and twenty minutes slip by. Her call count has sunk to the bottom of the team board, and her manager wants it up by Friday. She grabs a sticky pad, pen ready to write STOP in big letters.
examples.whatToDo: Write three lines instead: cue, a call ending in no; routine, the news site; reward, a break from the sting.
examples.whyItMatters: Once she sees a rejection sets it off, the lost minutes look like a loop she can work on, not laziness.

examples.title: A promise that lasted until Wednesday
examples.scenario: Mateo, sixteen, pulls out his phone in study hall whenever a chemistry problem stumps him. Last Sunday he vowed to quit cold for a week and deleted two games. By Wednesday he was scrolling again under the desk. Now the chemistry test is Friday, half the homework is undone, and he has a sinking sense that he just has no willpower.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the vow. Write down the cue (getting stuck on a problem), the routine (the phone) and the reward (relief from feeling stuck).
examples.whyItMatters: The trouble starts at being stuck, not at weak will, so that moment is where he can finally act.

examples.title: Shouting before the coat comes off
examples.scenario: Every evening Ruth trips over her son's football boots in the hall and starts shouting before her coat is off. Tonight he muttered, “You're always yelling,” and her face went hot. Part of her wants to insist it's his fault for leaving the boots there. Another part is ashamed that he is right, and she just wants the shouting to stop.
examples.whatToDo: Once the house is quiet, write the loop down: cue, tripping on the boots; routine, shouting; reward, feeling back in charge.
examples.whyItMatters: Naming the payoff calmly turns her shame into something she can study, so the next evening can go differently.

questions.prompt: Most mornings you stop at the same bakery on your walk to the train station and buy a pastry you meant to skip. You want to change this. What do you do this evening?
choices: Write down what sets off the stop, what you buy, and what it gives you.
Take a new walking route to the station so the bakery stays well out of sight.
Ask a friend to walk with you to the station every morning this week.
questions.explanation: Writing down the trigger, the purchase and the payoff shows you the loop before you try to change it. A new route or a walking buddy changes the morning while the loop itself stays unseen.

questions.prompt: A nurse wants to stop scrolling her phone on every break. She writes 'I scroll my phone' on a card and plans to read a book instead. Where is the trap in her plan?
choices: She picked a book, when a quieter phone game would be easier to swap in.
She quit in one go, when cutting back slowly would work better.
She wrote down the routine only, not the cue or the reward behind it.
questions.explanation: She named only the action. Without the cue that starts the scrolling and the reward it gives her, she is fighting a loop she can only partly see. Cutting back slowly leaves the same gap.

questions.prompt: A driver honks and mutters on his commute and has promised himself to stop. For a week he jots down where it happens, what he does and how he feels right after. What is he most likely to find?
choices: That it comes at random, so only more self-control will help.
That one stretch of road sets it off and venting gives him relief.
That he forgets his promise each morning and needs a note on the dash.
questions.explanation: A habit starts from a cue and pays off with a reward, so a week of notes tends to show both. Forgetting his promise is not the issue, since a habit can run without memory.

questions.prompt: A coworker tells you, “Every afternoon I end up at the office fridge for a soda. Starting Monday I'm switching to tea, full stop.” What is your best reply?
choices: “Track every drink you have for a whole month before you change a single thing.”
“Before Monday, write down what sends you there and what the soda gives you.”
“Keep the soda but drink half a can, so the switch is gentler.”
questions.explanation: Your coworker's plan swaps the drink before he knows what sends him to the fridge or what the soda gives him. Two quick notes fill that gap. A month of tracking only delays the change.

questions.prompt: A teenager kept losing her evenings to video games. She wrote down three things: finishing dinner, then gaming, then a break from thinking. Suddenly change felt doable. Why did writing it down help?
choices: It showed that finishing dinner starts it and the break keeps it going.
It made her feel guilty enough each night to put the game controller back down.
It helped her remember her goal each time the evening came around.
questions.explanation: Once she could see the cue and the reward, the gaming became a loop she could work on, not a weakness. Remembering her goal was not the issue, since the habit runs without her thinking brain fully taking part.

questions.prompt: Late most nights you end up browsing shopping apps in bed. You've written down the routine and a guess at the reward, but what sets it off is still unclear. What should you do next?
choices: Keep a paperback by the bed and read it instead whenever the urge shows up.
List your other daily habits too, so you see the whole picture.
Note the time, the place and your mood each night, until a pattern shows.
questions.explanation: You can't work on a loop while its trigger is still a guess. Noting the time, place and mood each night soon shows what starts the browsing. Reading instead changes the routine before you know the cue.

questions.prompt: A man writes down his late-night email habit. Cue: plugging in his phone by the bed. Routine: checking work email. Reward: none, since it only makes him tense. What trap has he fallen into?
choices: Writing none for the reward, when something must keep the email check going.
Mapping the habit first, when moving the charger out of the room is quicker.
Choosing such a small habit, when a bigger one would matter more.
questions.explanation: A loop that keeps running is paying him something, or his brain would not keep it. Writing none hides the part he most needs to see. Moving the charger changes a loop he has only half mapped.

reviewCards.front: You buy a candy bar from the office vending machine every afternoon and want to quit.
reviewCards.back: Before you change anything, write down what sets off the trip, what you do and what the candy gives you, so you know what you are up against.

reviewCards.front: Why does sheer willpower so often lose to an old habit?
reviewCards.back: Because once a habit forms, the thinking part of your brain stops fully taking part. The loop runs on its own until you see its cue and its reward.

reviewCards.front: Before you try to replace a habit with a better one, the first thing to put on paper is ...
reviewCards.back: ... its cue, its routine and its reward, so you can see the whole loop you are about to change.

reviewCards.front: Someone wanted to stop staying up late watching shows. They wrote one line, 'too much TV', set a strict bedtime and slipped within days. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: They named only the routine. Without the cue that starts it and the reward that keeps it going, they were fighting a loop they could only half see.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what is the first step in changing a habit, and why?
reviewCards.back: Map the habit loop. Write down what triggers it, what you do and what you get, because a habit runs on its own and you can only change what you can see.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting the trigger, the action and the payoff behind a habit before trying to change it.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I walk in the door after work and put my bag down, I write down what I do in the next ten minutes and what I get from it.
When I catch myself doing the very habit I promised to stop, I write down what happened right before it and how I feel right now.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, catch your chosen habit once as it happens. Note the time, the place and your mood just before, and what you felt right after.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each evening this week, add one line to your habit note: when it started, what you did and what you got. On the weekend, circle the cue that shows up most.

chapters.title: Why Some New Habits Stick and Others Fade
chapters.hook: Lacing up your shoes every morning for a month won't make running a habit. Wanting what comes after the run will.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels natural to expect that anything you repeat enough will turn into a habit. But repeating is not enough, because a habit takes hold only when your brain starts wanting the reward as soon as the cue appears.
chapters.keyTakeaway: To build a habit, pick one obvious cue and one clear reward, then let yourself start craving that reward.
chapters.tryThisNow: Set your workout shoes beside your bed tonight, right where your feet will land in the morning.

memorableLines.text: A habit sticks when the cue alone makes you hungry for the reward.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why do some people keep running every morning for years, while most quit after two weeks? Both groups mean well. Charles Duhigg says the ones who last have learned to crave something. A craving is the wanting that switches on the moment a cue, the signal that starts a habit, shows up.

A scientist, Wolfram Schultz, gave a monkey named Julio a drop of juice each time Julio pulled a lever when a shape flashed on a screen. At first, Julio's brain gave a burst of activity only when the juice arrived. After many rounds, the burst came as soon as the shape appeared, before any juice. When the juice did not come, his brain showed something like frustration. Duhigg says people who stick with exercise do the same. They pick one plain cue, like running shoes by the bed, and one clear reward, like a treat or the proud feeling of being done. Soon the shoes alone make them want that reward.

Repeating the run does not build that pull. A vague reward, like getting fit someday, gives your brain nothing to expect when the alarm rings, so each run starts as a fresh fight. Once you pair one obvious cue with one clear reward and let yourself crave it, you become one of the people who keep going.

breakdown.fullRead:
Why do some people keep running every morning for years, while most quit after two weeks? Both groups mean well. They buy the shoes, set the alarm and head out on the first day full of hope. A few weeks later, one group is still on the road at dawn. The other has stopped without ever quite deciding to.

Charles Duhigg says the ones who last have learned to crave something. A craving is the wanting that switches on the moment a cue, the signal that starts a habit, shows up. You already know that a cue leads to a routine and then a reward. That alone does not make a new habit stick. The habit takes hold once your brain starts to expect the reward and long for it, and that longing is what powers the whole thing.

A scientist, Wolfram Schultz, saw this happen inside a monkey named Julio. Julio sat facing a screen while Schultz recorded the activity in the monkey's brain. Each time a shape appeared and Julio pulled a lever, a drop of juice ran onto his lips. At first, his brain gave a burst of activity only when the juice arrived. The good feeling came with the reward, and not a moment before.

After many rounds, something changed. The burst came as soon as the shape appeared, before any juice reached him. The shape had turned into a promise. When the juice came late or not at all, Julio's brain showed something like frustration. He had not just learned that shapes meant juice. He had come to want the juice the instant he saw the shape, and that wanting now pulled him toward the lever.

Claude Hopkins, an advertising man, put the same pull to work selling a toothpaste called Pepsodent. He told people to run their tongue across their teeth and notice the film on them. That film is always there, so the cue was waiting whenever someone checked. The paste also held ingredients that made the mouth tingle. People came to crave that tingle, and Pepsodent became a huge seller.

Procter & Gamble learned the same thing the hard way. The company made a spray called Febreze that could take bad smells away, and at first it flopped. The people living with the worst smells had stopped noticing them. With no smell to notice, there was no cue to reach for the spray. Then researchers watched people clean their homes. Febreze was relaunched with a pleasant scent, sold as the finishing touch at the end of cleaning. That fresh smell became a reward people looked forward to, and sales took off.

Duhigg says people who stick with exercise do the same thing. They pick one plain cue, like running shoes by the bed, and one clear reward, like a treat or the proud feeling of being done. At first the reward is just something nice at the end. After a while, the sight of the shoes alone makes them want it. From then on, getting out the door takes far less of a push.

It seems as if doing something often enough should turn it into a habit. Repeating the run does not build that pull. A vague reward, like getting fit someday, gives your brain nothing to expect when the alarm rings, so each run starts as a fresh fight. A cue you barely notice fails too, the way Febreze did at first. Once you pair one obvious cue with one clear reward and let yourself crave it, you become one of the people who keep going.

examples.title: A swim plan around the kitchen table
examples.scenario: Jonah and two old school friends want to start swimming laps together twice a week. He can already picture the group chat every night, full of "who's in?" and excuses. They're sitting around his kitchen table with the pool's opening times on his phone. Elif leans back and asks how they'll keep this going past the first month.
examples.whatToDo: Agree on one cue, meeting at the pool gate when it opens on Tuesdays and Fridays, and one reward, warm bagels together at the shop next door.
examples.whyItMatters: Once the open gate means bagels with friends, they'll want to go, and nobody has to chase anyone in the chat.

examples.title: The café owner's nightly paperwork
examples.scenario: Soraya owns a small café and wants to go through each day's sales and bills before she heads home. For three weeks she forced herself to sit at the counter every night, tired and grumbling, sure it would turn automatic. It never did. She skipped a night, then a week, and last Friday a supplier charged her a late fee she hadn't seen coming.
examples.whatToDo: Make flipping the door sign to Closed her cue, and keep the day's last cinnamon bun for herself once the bills are done.
examples.whyItMatters: Three weeks of forcing gave her nothing to look forward to. A treat at the end lets the Closed sign start pulling her.

examples.title: When the mentor scoffs at treats
examples.scenario: Teodoro is an apprentice carpenter learning to cut joints by hand. His mentor, Gudrun, wants one practice joint cut at the bench every morning before the saws start up. Teodoro asks if he can reward each good joint with a coffee from the truck parked outside. Gudrun laughs. "Treats are for kids. Just cut one every day until your hands know it." He feels silly for asking.
examples.whatToDo: Keep Gudrun's cue, the bench before the saws start, and quietly buy that coffee after each finished joint without needing her blessing.
examples.whyItMatters: Her cue is a good one, but with nothing to look forward to after it, he has no reason to start wanting the bench.

questions.prompt: A man buys a secondhand guitar and plays for ten minutes every evening after dinner. The payoff, he tells himself, is playing at his sister's wedding next year. Three weeks in, he skips more nights than he plays. What trap did he fall into?
choices: Practicing after dinner, when he is too tired to focus well
Counting on a reward a year away, not one he gets tonight
Keeping each session too short to build real skill
questions.explanation: After dinner works fine as a cue. The trouble is the reward, a wedding a year off, so tonight's ten minutes end with nothing he can feel or start to want. Longer sessions would only make each evening harder.

questions.prompt: A woman keeps her yoga mat rolled out beside the kettle. While the water boils, she stretches. Only after that does she carry her first coffee out to the balcony. What is most likely true two months later?
choices: She feels pulled toward the mat as soon as she fills the kettle
She stretches only on mornings when she feels full of energy
She still needs a reminder on her phone each morning before she starts stretching
questions.explanation: Filling the kettle is a cue she can't miss, and the balcony coffee is a reward she feels right away, so the kettle starts the wanting. A phone reminder adds nothing once the kettle does that job.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I go to the gym straight after work, but I dread every session, and I'm skipping more each week." What's the best thing to say back?
choices: "Go in the morning instead, when you have more energy to spare."
"Push through a few more weeks; habits just take time."
"Save one treat you really love for right after each workout."
questions.explanation: Straight after work is already a clear cue. What's missing is a reward to look forward to, so nothing pulls your friend in. More weeks of dread would just repeat the same fight.

questions.prompt: A twelve-year-old dodged piano practice for months. Her dad set a bowl of clementines on the piano lid, and she gets one only after twenty minutes of playing. A few weeks later she sits down without being asked. Why did the change work?
choices: Sitting at the piano began to make her want the clementine
Twenty minutes was short enough that she stopped resisting it
The bowl on the lid reminded her that practice was due
questions.explanation: The clementine is a clear reward right after practice, so the piano itself began to set off the wanting. A bowl that only reminded her would be a cue with nothing behind it.

questions.prompt: You've promised yourself a short walk sometime each afternoon, followed by an iced tea from the corner shop. Some days the walk happens. Most days the afternoon slips away. What do you change first?
choices: Walk whenever you feel restless, so it fits your mood that day
Start the walk at one set moment, right after lunch ends
Trade the iced tea for a bigger treat worth chasing
questions.explanation: The iced tea is a clear reward, but sometime each afternoon is no cue, so nothing sets off the wanting. Tying the walk to the end of lunch fixes that. A bigger treat would still float free.

questions.prompt: A woman wants to take a vitamin every morning. She leaves the bottle on the spice shelf, where it has stood since spring, and promises herself a square of dark chocolate after each one. A week later the bottle is nearly full. Where did her plan go wrong?
choices: Choosing chocolate, a reward too small to really matter
Picking a habit too dull to hold her interest
Leaving the bottle where her eyes slide right past it
questions.explanation: A bottle she has looked past for months is no cue, so the chocolate never gets a moment to be wanted. A bigger reward wouldn't help while nothing catches her eye each morning.

questions.prompt: For a year, a man has ended every evening run on his porch with a glass of cold sparkling water. Tonight he gets back and finds the fridge empty. What is he most likely to feel?
choices: He barely notices, since running is automatic by now
He feels a sharp letdown, as if something owed is missing
He feels proud that he finished the run without the usual reward
questions.explanation: After a year, the end of the run sets off the wanting before the glass is in his hand, so its absence stings. A run so automatic that the reward no longer matters misses what kept him going.

reviewCards.front: Why does a new habit need a reward you can feel right away, and not only lots of repeats?
reviewCards.back: Because it sticks once the cue alone makes you want that reward. With nothing to look forward to, each repeat is a fresh fight.

reviewCards.front: The cue for a new habit works best when it is ...
reviewCards.back: ... something you can't miss at the moment it matters, like a yoga mat beside the kettle, so the wanting has a clear place to start.

reviewCards.front: A man went to a Thursday dance class for two months, gritting his teeth every time, sure it would turn into a habit. Then he quit. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He counted on repeats alone. With no reward he looked forward to after class, Thursday never began to pull him toward the door.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what makes a new habit finally stick?
reviewCards.back: One clear trigger, one reward you feel soon after, and enough rounds for the trigger to start making you want that reward.

reviewCards.front: You open a language app at random times, finish a lesson and feel nothing. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Tie the lesson to one fixed moment, like your first sip of coffee, and give yourself a small reward right after, until the coffee itself makes you want it.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Tying a new routine to a trigger you can't miss and a payoff you look forward to.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking I should restart something I keep dropping, I choose one cue I can't miss and one reward I'll get right after it.
When I walk in the door at home after work, I do my new habit as soon as I see its cue, and take my reward straight after.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, do your new habit once right after its cue, then take your reward straight away and notice how good it feels.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Keep the same cue and the same reward every day this week. On the last day, notice whether the cue alone has started to make you look forward to the reward.

chapters.title: Keep the Trigger, Keep the Payoff, Change the Action
chapters.hook: Every night you swear you'll stop snacking after dinner. Then nine o'clock comes, the urge arrives on time, and your hands have nothing to do.
chapters.counterintuition: You have probably been told that quitting a bad habit takes willpower and a firm stop. The trouble is the trigger still arrives and your brain still wants the payoff, so keep both and swap only what you do in between.
chapters.keyTakeaway: To change a habit, keep the same trigger and the same payoff, and swap only what you do.
chapters.tryThisNow: Tell one person today which moment sets off a habit you want to change, and what new action could give you the same payoff.

memorableLines.text: Same trigger, same payoff, new action in between.

breakdown.fastRead:
You can't wipe out a bad habit. You can only change it. Charles Duhigg calls this the golden rule of habit change. Keep the trigger, the moment that sets the habit off, and the payoff, the good feeling it brings. Swap only what you do in between. Alcoholics Anonymous works this way. Drinkers keep their old triggers and the relief and company they were after. Meetings and a sponsor, a more experienced member, take the drink's place.

Mandy, a graduate student, bit her nails until they bled. Her trigger was a tense feeling in her fingertips, and she marked a card each time it came. When it struck, she put her hands in her pockets or rubbed her arm. That gave her fingers a quick physical feeling in place of the biting, and the biting faded. Quitting by force feels right because the habit looks like the problem. Yet the trigger keeps coming, and your brain still wants the payoff. Just stop, and the urge has nowhere to go.

So start by marking each time the trigger hits. Then name what the habit really gives you, like relief or company. examples.title: A snapped bolt at ten in the morning
examples.scenario: Tomasz runs a two-bay car garage. Whenever a job goes wrong, he wipes his hands on a red rag and walks out back for a cigarette and five quiet minutes. He has promised his daughter he'll quit by summer. It's ten in the morning, a rusted bolt has just snapped under his wrench, and the rag is already in his hand.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the walk out back and the five quiet minutes, but carry a mug of coffee out there instead of a cigarette.
examples.whyItMatters: Stuck jobs will keep coming, and this way he still gets his quiet break without lighting up.

examples.title: Skipping the bakery after the Sunday walk
examples.scenario: Every Sunday morning, Jelena walks the canal path with four neighbours, and the walk ends at the corner bakery with almond croissants. Three weeks ago, to cut back, she began heading straight home after the walk. Since then she has missed the chat and the plans for the street party, and has eaten half a packet of biscuits alone at her kitchen table.
examples.whatToDo: Go to the bakery with the group, sit at the same table, and order a pot of tea instead of a croissant.
examples.whyItMatters: Sitting with the group keeps the company she was really after, so the croissant is easier to skip.

examples.title: The cello piece that keeps starting over
examples.scenario: Noor is learning the cello, and her spring recital is six weeks away. Every time she plays a wrong note, she stops and starts the piece from the top. Her teacher suggested she keep playing through mistakes instead. She tried it at her last lesson, but the sour note nagged at her for the rest of the piece. By the next week she was restarting again.
examples.whatToDo: Keep playing through the wrong note, then play that one bar again the moment the piece ends, so it still gets put right.
examples.whyItMatters: Restarting gave her the feeling of fixing the mistake, and the new move only sticks if it gives her that too.

questions.prompt: Every afternoon at three, a warehouse worker gets sleepy and buys a candy bar from the machine. He starts taking a brisk lap of the loading dock at three instead. What most likely happens over the next few weeks?
choices: He soon misses the candy, because a lap of the dock has no sugar in it.
The sleepy dip at three stops coming, so there is nothing left to crave.
The lap gives him the same lift, so the candy bar slowly loses its pull.
questions.explanation: The sleepy dip still comes at three, but now the lap answers it with the same lift the candy gave. The dip doesn't vanish, so what changes is only what he does about it.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "Whenever my boss sends a sharp email, I walk to the shop for a snack to calm down. I'm just going to stop." What is your best reply?
choices: "Then leave your boss's emails unread until the end of the day."
"What calms you about that trip? Find another way to get that calm."
"Good plan. Buy yourself something nice at the end of each week you manage."
questions.explanation: The sharp emails will keep coming, and your friend still needs to calm down. Another way to get that calm, right then, does the snack's job. A weekly treat arrives days too late to help.

questions.prompt: A teenager used to open a video game whenever homework got hard. She began noting those moments on a sticky note. Now, when one comes, she shoots ten hoops in the driveway, then sits back down. The game habit has faded. Why did the change stick?
choices: The hoops give her the same short break the game did, right when she needs it.
Writing the moments down showed her the problem, and seeing it clearly was enough to stop it.
Going outside kept her away from the screen, so the game lost its pull.
questions.explanation: Hard homework still comes, and she still wants a short break from it. The hoops give her that break at the same moment. Writing the moments down helped her spot them, but it didn't fill them.

questions.prompt: You chew the inside of your cheek in long meetings and want to change it. You aren't sure yet what sets it off. Where do you start?
choices: Chew gum in meetings so your mouth has something else to do.
Ask a coworker to give you a quiet nudge whenever they see you doing it.
Mark your notes each time you catch yourself, and jot what just happened.
questions.explanation: You can't pick a good swap until you know what sets the chewing off and what it gives you. Marking each time shows you both. Gum right now is a guess made too early.

questions.prompt: After every late shift, a cook pours a beer to unwind. To cut back, she starts doing the laundry the moment she gets home instead. Two weeks later, the beer is back. Where was the trap?
choices: She only did the laundry on some nights, so the swap never set in.
She should have skipped the swap and pushed through on willpower.
Laundry kept her busy, but it didn't help her unwind like the beer.
questions.explanation: The beer gave her a way to unwind after a hard shift. Laundry filled the moment but gave her no rest, so the old pull stayed. Willpower alone would leave that urge with nowhere to go.

questions.prompt: A student bites her pen whenever she gets stuck on a maths problem. To break it, she squeezes a stress ball for five minutes every evening. What happens to the pen biting?
choices: She keeps biting it when stuck, since the ball never shows up at that moment.
It slowly fades, since squeezing the ball gives her hands the same relief the pen did.
It eases a little, since the evening squeezes slowly calm her nervous hands.
questions.explanation: Getting stuck is her trigger, and that's when her hands want relief. A ball squeezed in the evening misses that moment, so the pen still does the job. The swap has to happen when the trigger strikes.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "Every lunch break I end up gossiping about coworkers with the same colleague, and afterward I feel awful. So I'll eat alone at my desk from now on." What do you tell them?
choices: "Keep the lunches, and just bite your tongue whenever gossip starts."
"Keep the lunches together, and steer the talk toward weekends and plans."
"Allow yourself one bit of gossip a day, so you don't feel deprived."
questions.explanation: Lunch with that colleague is the trigger, and the company is the payoff. Keeping both and changing the topic swaps out only the gossip. Biting your tongue leaves the urge with nothing to do.

reviewCards.front: Before you choose a new action to replace an old habit, first ...
reviewCards.back: ... mark each time the habit's trigger hits and name what the habit gives you, so the new action can give the same thing.

reviewCards.front: Someone stopped scrolling on the bus to work by leaving their phone at home. A week later they were scrolling again. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: They took the scrolling away but gave the ride nothing else to do. The bus ride and the wish for a distraction were still there, so a book or a crossword needed to fill that slot.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, how do you change a habit you can't simply stop?
reviewCards.back: Leave alone the moment that sets it off and the good feeling it gives, and find a new action for that moment that gives the same feeling.

reviewCards.front: Every time a work call goes badly, you open the fridge, mostly for a minute to yourself. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Keep the minute to yourself after the call, but spend it another way, like stepping out onto the balcony or making a cup of tea.

reviewCards.front: Why does a new action only stick if it gives the same payoff as the old habit?
reviewCards.back: Because the trigger keeps coming and you still want the payoff. If the new action doesn't give you that, the old habit is still the only way to get it.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting what sets off a habit and what it gives you, then filling that moment with a new action that gives the same thing.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself halfway into a habit I want to change, I note what happened just before and what I was hoping to feel.
When I get home from work and feel like switching off, I get that same rest from a new action, like a short walk, not my old habit.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one habit you want to change and make a mark on a scrap of paper each time its trigger hits today. Next to each mark, write what you wanted right then.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each week, look over your marks. Name the payoff they point to, choose one new action that gives the same thing, and use it every time the trigger hits the week after.

chapters.title: Change the One Habit That Moves All the Others
chapters.hook: The whiteboard by your front door holds eight new rules for Monday. By Friday, all eight come off with one swipe.
chapters.counterintuition: To change your life, you have to fix everything at once. It sounds right, and it fails for one reason: habits are tied together, so fighting each one alone wastes your effort. Change the one that pulls the others, and they follow.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Pick one habit that touches many others, change only that, and let the rest follow.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one line naming the single habit that would pull your other goals along, and stick it where you'll see it tonight.

memorableLines.text: Change the habit the others hang on, and the rest come along.

It is Sunday night, and Nkechi is filling a new planner with eight rules for Monday. Her last two fresh starts looked like this, and both died by Friday. Each one left her trusting herself less.

Fixing everything at once feels brave. It fails because each rule becomes its own daily fight. Charles Duhigg says to aim instead at a keystone habit, one habit that sets off a chain reaction and reshapes others. When Paul O'Neill became head of Alcoa, a huge aluminum company, he told investors his top goal was worker safety, not profit. Any injury had to reach him within a day, with a plan to stop it happening again. To meet that rule, news had to race from the factory floor to the top. Those new lines of talk changed how the whole company ran. Alcoa's profits hit records. In one study, people asked to write down what they ate lost more weight, because the journal got them planning meals.

So ask which habit would pull the others along if it changed. Nkechi crosses out seven rules and keeps one: write down everything she spends. Takeout looks worse on paper, so she cooks more and saves more. People change most when they change one habit that touches many others and let the rest follow.

At the Beijing Olympics, Phelps's goggles filled with water during a race. He could not see, so he swam by counting his strokes. He won gold and set a world record. A few small routines had shaped how he handled everything else in the water.

Writing things down was the one change, and better eating grew out of it. To find your own, ask which habit on your list would pull the others along if it changed. It is often a small one that sits underneath the rest.

Takeout looks worse on paper, so she starts cooking more. The money she stops spending turns into the savings she had planned to force. By Friday the one rule is still standing. examples.title: Overdrawn again on the 24th
examples.scenario: On the 24th, Matteo's bank app shows him overdrawn again. He opens a notebook and lists six fixes: cancel streaming, a grocery budget, no lunches out, no afternoon coffee run, sell his old guitar, pay down the card. Most of his money leaks between noon and four at work. It is ten at night, and he has to pick where to start.
examples.whatToDo: Pack tomorrow's lunch tonight and leave the other five fixes alone. Start there, because lunch sits inside the noon-to-four hours when most of the money leaks.
examples.whyItMatters: One ten-minute evening job plugs the noon-to-four leak, so the grocery plan and the card payment get easier on their own.

examples.title: A homework chart torn off the wall
examples.scenario: After a poor report card, Rafael taped a chart above his daughter Amara's desk: math sheets every day, twenty minutes of reading, no tablet on school nights, bed by nine. Three weeks in, every evening ends in shouting. Last night she ripped the chart down and told him she hates school now.
examples.whatToDo: Take the chart down for good and keep one habit: ten minutes each evening going through her school planner together.
examples.whyItMatters: Looking at the planner each night brings homework, tests and reading into one calm talk, so the rest can follow without a fight.

examples.title: Five minutes to fix a night shift
examples.scenario: Dagny has just taken charge of night shifts at a care home with a long list of problems: late medicines, falls, lost notes and families waiting for calls. Her manager wants all of it fixed. She gets one five-minute huddle before tonight's shift, and twelve tired staff are already watching the clock.
examples.whatToDo: Spend the five minutes on one change: every handover happens at the resident's bedside, with both nurses there.
examples.whyItMatters: At the bedside, staff catch late medicines, fall risks and family messages in one look, so one habit reaches the whole list.

questions.prompt: A coworker tells you she is starting a new life on Monday: running, cooking, budgeting, early nights and guitar lessons. What's the best reply?
choices: "Ask which of the five would drag the rest along, and start there."
"Write down why each of them matters to you, so the reasons keep you going."
"Start with the hardest one, since the easy ones can come later."
questions.explanation: Starting with the one habit that pulls the others along means one daily fight instead of five. Writing reasons for all five still leaves five fights running on the same Monday.

questions.prompt: A bus driver wanted to eat better, stop buying snacks and feel less tired. He changed only one thing: lights out by ten. Months later, all three had improved. What explains it?
choices: Bed by ten was easy, so he had energy left for the rest.
Going to bed earlier changed his mornings, which changed how he ate and spent.
Sleep matters more than any other habit, so fixing it fixes every other problem too.
questions.explanation: An earlier bedtime reshaped his mornings, and his eating and snack buying moved with them. Sleep being the most important habit is not what did it. The bedtime worked because it touched the other two.

questions.prompt: You've just become shift lead at a warehouse where orders ship late, pallets get the wrong labels and nobody speaks up about problems. Your first team meeting is tomorrow morning. What's your move there?
choices: Hand out a full plan that tackles late orders, wrong labels and the silence all at once.
Set a weekly target for on-time orders and post the results by the door.
Ask that every mix-up reach you the same day, with an idea to stop it.
questions.explanation: A same-day report on every mix-up opens a line from the floor to you, and that line touches labels, late orders and silence. A plan for all three at once means three daily fights.

questions.prompt: A student's term is a mess: late nights, homework done at midnight and hours on her phone. She picks one change, a color-coded pencil case, because it is the easiest she can think of. Weeks later, nothing else has shifted. Where did she go wrong?
choices: She picked the easiest change, not one that touches the rest of her week.
She should have tackled the late nights, the homework and the phone all at once.
She needed a small treat each day the pencil case stayed neat.
questions.explanation: A neat pencil case touches nothing else, so nothing else moved. A change like an earlier bedtime could have pulled the late nights, homework and phone along. A daily treat keeps the pencil case neat but changes nothing more.

questions.prompt: A family keeps fighting about money, chores and screen time. They start one habit: a ten-minute talk every Sunday evening to plan the week, with phones in a basket. What most likely happens over the next few months?
choices: The talks calm things down, but only for a day or two.
The talks turn into a weekly blame session that makes the fights worse.
Planning together starts to settle the chores, money and screen fights too.
questions.explanation: Planning the week together gives chores, money and screens one calm place to come up, so all three start to shift. The talk keeps working because it happens every week, not just once.

questions.prompt: You and your partner have kept one new habit for a month: a Sunday walk where you plan the week together. Since the walks began, you've both gone to bed earlier and spent less without trying. Your partner says, "It's working. Let's add a budget and a sleep rule this week." How do you answer?
choices: "Let's add one a month, once the walk feels easy."
"Let's keep only the walk for now and see what it changes."
"Let's track the walk in an app so we don't miss a week."
questions.explanation: The walk is already moving your bedtimes and spending, the very things the budget and sleep rule are for. Adding rules now only adds fights the walk is winning without them.

questions.prompt: A new manager at a call center made one rule: every customer complaint gets read aloud at the morning huddle. Within a year, wait times fell, training improved and fewer staff quit. Why did one rule reach so far?
choices: Hearing the complaints every morning made staff too scared to make mistakes.
The rule was so simple that every person on every shift could remember it.
Talking about complaints each morning brought waits, training and staffing problems into view.
questions.explanation: Going over complaints each morning opened a daily line where wait times, training gaps and staff worries came up and got fixed. A simple rule is easy to remember, but being simple does not change anything else.

reviewCards.front: A new team leader tried to fix lateness, sloppy reports and long meetings in her first week. A month later, all three were the same. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She opened three fights at once. One change that touched all three, such as a short daily check-in, could have pulled the rest along.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what is the move when you want many parts of your life to change?
reviewCards.back: Pick the one habit the others hang on, change only that, and give the rest time to follow.

reviewCards.front: Your evenings go to scrolling, takeout and late bedtimes, and you want all three gone. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Pick the habit sitting under the others, like charging your phone in the hall at eight, and change only that. Less scrolling can bring cooking and earlier sleep with it.

reviewCards.front: Why can changing one well-chosen habit change others you never touched?
reviewCards.back: Some habits set off a chain reaction. Moving one changes what happens around it, so the linked habits shift without a fight of their own.

reviewCards.front: When a list of fixes keeps growing, the first step is to ...
reviewCards.back: ... ask which one habit would pull the others along, and cross out the rest for now.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting the one routine your other routines lean on, and putting all your effort there.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to plan my week, I circle the one habit that would pull my other goals along and work only on that.
When I catch myself thinking I need to fix everything at once, I cross out every goal but the one habit that touches the most others.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, list every habit you want to change. Draw a line from each one to any other it affects, then circle the one with the most lines.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each evening this week, check whether you kept your one habit and note one other thing that shifted without effort. Start no second habit until the week is over.

chapters.title: Plan Your Weakest Moment Before It Arrives
chapters.hook: Same long day, same chips in the cupboard. Why does one person cave by nine while another, who wrote two lines at breakfast, doesn't?
chapters.counterintuition: The usual advice is to grit your teeth when the hard moment comes. Deciding on paper beforehand what you'll do works better, because willpower tires like a muscle, and by that moment yours is already worn down.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Pick the moment you usually cave, and write down ahead of time exactly what you will do then.
chapters.tryThisNow: Open your phone's notes now and write one line: the moment today you're most likely to give in, and exactly what you'll do then.

memorableLines.text: Decide on paper while you're calm, so the hard moment has nothing left to decide.

breakdown.fastRead:
Travis Leach grew up with parents addicted to drugs, and he kept losing jobs when he lost his temper. Later he was managing a Starbucks store. What changed?

Charles Duhigg's answer is that willpower is a habit, built by deciding ahead what you'll do at the hard moment. The reason is that willpower tires like a muscle. In one study, people told to eat radishes and not touch nearby cookies quit a later puzzle sooner than people who ate the cookies. Starbucks trains new workers to write down what they'll do at the moments they're most likely to slip, then to practice it. For an angry customer, they listen, acknowledge the complaint, take action, thank the person and explain why it happened. With routines like that, Travis held his job and became a manager. In two hospitals in Scotland, older patients recovering from hip or knee surgery wrote plans for the painful moments. They started walking faster than patients who didn't.

Gritting your teeth fails because the hard moment is when the muscle is most tired. A plan written earlier, while you're calm, has already done the choosing. When you know the moment you usually cave, write down now exactly what you'll do then, and you'll hold steady even when your willpower runs out.
breakdown.deepRead:
Travis Leach grew up with parents addicted to drugs. As a young man he kept losing jobs, and the reason was always the same. He lost his temper, and then he lost the job. Later he was managing a Starbucks store. What had he found that he had been missing?

Charles Duhigg's answer is that willpower is a habit you can build, not a gift you're born with or without. He calls it the most important keystone habit for success, meaning one habit that pulls many others along with it. You build it by deciding ahead of time what you'll do when things get hard. The reason is that willpower tires like a muscle. In one study, people told to eat radishes and not touch nearby cookies quit a later puzzle sooner than people who ate the cookies. Holding back had used up their strength.

Duhigg has a name for the moments of pain or temptation where willpower tends to break. He calls them inflection points. Starbucks has new workers write down what they'll do at each one, then practice until it runs on its own. For an angry customer, the routine is to listen, acknowledge the complaint, take action, thank the person, and explain why it happened. Starbucks calls it LATTE, after the first letter of each step. Travis learned routines like these. He held his job and became a store manager. The same idea works far from a coffee counter. Travis Leach grew up with parents who were addicted to drugs. As a young man he kept losing jobs, and the reason was always the same. Charles Duhigg's answer is that willpower is a habit, not a gift you are born with or without. He calls it the single most important keystone habit for doing well in life, meaning a habit that pulls many others along with it. Like any habit, it can be built. You build it by deciding ahead of time what you'll do when the hard moment comes, so the choice is already made.

Your willpower drains the same way through a long day, and each time you hold back, a little less is left.

Duhigg reports one more finding about that drain. People who were asked politely and given a reason for a task used less willpower doing it than people who were simply ordered around. Being treated as someone in charge of their own choices made the effort cost them less.

examples.title: A layout that breaks every afternoon
examples.scenario: Femi builds websites for clients from a desk in his spare room. Whenever a page layout breaks, he clicks over to the news and loses the afternoon. Today a florist's homepage is due by six, and the layout is the tricky part. It's nine in the morning. He opens his task list, coffee in hand, ready to start.
examples.whatToDo: At the top of the list, he writes what he'll do when a layout breaks: fix one box, refresh the page, then take the next.
examples.whyItMatters: By afternoon his patience will be worn thin, but the next step will already be waiting on the page.

examples.title: Shutting the laptop after one wrong answer
examples.scenario: Lucía takes an online bookkeeping course at night, after her shift. Whenever she gets a practice question wrong, she shuts the laptop. Her fix has been to tell herself to tough it out. Last week she sat at the screen for an hour, forcing herself to stay, and finished nothing. Now she is three lessons behind and dreads opening the course.
examples.whatToDo: Before tonight's lesson, she writes what she'll do after a wrong answer: read the explanation once, then try the next question.
examples.whyItMatters: Forcing herself burned what little willpower her shift had left. A step chosen earlier only has to be followed.

examples.title: Greasy pans waiting after work

Last Thursday he slammed a cupboard and said things he regretted, and they barely spoke all weekend. Just thinking about tonight's sink makes his jaw tighten.

examples.whyItMatters: His anger will be at full heat by the sink, so the words have to be picked while he's still cool.

questions.prompt: A city bus driver used to snap at passengers in the last hour of her route. She wrote down what she'd say when that hour came, and the snapping stopped. What made the written lines work?

Her self-control was worn out by then, but the plan had already decided for her.
Reading the words each day reminded her why calm mattered, so the urge to snap faded.

Write a plan each morning for how you'll spend your whole workday.
Write down what you'll say and do at noon when they ask you along.
questions.explanation: Noon, when the invite comes, is where you give in, so that's where the written plan belongs. A strict month-long rule still leaves you fighting alone at noon on tired willpower.

Bedtime is the hardest hour, so change should start with an easier part of the day.
The note hangs on the busy fridge, where everyone soon stops noticing it.

When the topic comes up, she falls back on her planned move.
Planning for the fight ahead just gets her more worked up.

Patients can tell she won't be pushed around, so they ease off sooner.
The steps were chosen when she was calm, so a tired mind just follows them.

Set the written plan aside, and next Sunday just push harder to stay calm.
Skip the next few Sunday dinners until things between you cool down.

chapters.title: Fix Old Habits While the Crisis Is Fresh
chapters.hook: Your team is still rereading the angry client email, and everyone says to let things cool off. Cooling off is how nothing changes.

chapters.keyTakeaway: When something goes badly wrong, use that moment to change the routines everyone has been putting up with.
chapters.tryThisNow: Set a blank page beside your laptop today and title it Things We Put Up With.

A team's worst week is often the best time to fix its habits. That sounds backwards. When something goes badly wrong, the usual instinct is to let people calm down and fix the system later, with cooler heads. Charles Duhigg argues the opposite, and his evidence comes from places where waiting cost lives.

At Rhode Island Hospital, nurses and surgeons had settled into an unspoken peace deal, which Duhigg calls a truce. Many surgeons expected to be obeyed, and nurses had learned to give way rather than fight them. Nurses kept their own quiet ways of warning each other about difficult surgeons. The deal kept the days running. It also meant a nurse with a worry had no easy way to stop an operation.

Before an old man's brain surgery, a nurse raised a doubt about which side of his head the operation was meant to be on. The surgeon brushed it off and went ahead. He operated on the wrong side, and the man died. The truce had done what it was built to do. It kept the peace, and it let a danger slip past. More errors followed at the hospital. Only then did its leaders tear up the old safety habits and build new ones.

A fire at London's King's Cross station shows the same pattern in a different place. The station was run by separate departments, and each kept to its own patch. Each assumed that safety belonged to someone else. Rubbish had piled up under an escalator, and that is where the fire started. It killed dozens of people.

The investigator, Desmond Fennell, looked for the person in charge of keeping passengers safe and found there was none. Each department looked after its own job, and the gaps between them belonged to nobody. He used the shock of the fire to push through new rules the old system had resisted. His report changed how the stations were run.

Why does waiting feel right? People are hurt and angry, and a cool head seems wiser. But Duhigg says every organization runs on habits, which he calls routines. They are the unwritten ways of doing things that let work get done without a fresh decision every hour. They also hold the truces between rival groups in place, so most of the time they barely move. Nobody wants to restart old fights.

A crisis changes that for a short while. Suddenly everyone can see the danger, and the old deals stop looking safe. Good leaders, Duhigg says, grab that moment to remake how the group works. Some even make a crisis feel bigger than it is, or keep the sense of crisis going longer, so the window stays open. Wait for calm, and the routines set again, with the old problem still inside them.

So keep a list of problems everyone shrugs off, at work or at home. When something breaks, check the list for the routine behind it. Ask who was meant to look after it, and whether anyone really was. Then gather people and change it that week, while they still care. Change what everyone puts up with in the week something breaks, and the fix will last.

examples.title: Lights out over an unpaid bill
examples.scenario: Dalia and her partner Paulo drop every bill into a wicker basket on the microwave, and each quietly assumes the other has paid. Tonight the lights cut out. The power company has cut them off over a bill nobody paid. Paulo lights a candle. He says it can wait till the weekend, once they've both calmed down. Dalia looks at the basket.
examples.whatToDo: Sit down by the candle tonight, empty the basket together, and agree who pays which bill from now on.
examples.whyItMatters: Tonight both of them care about the bills. By the weekend, assuming the other one paid will feel normal again.

examples.title: A pallet slides off the truck again
examples.scenario: Gustavo runs the morning shift at a parcel depot. Last month a pallet slid off a truck on the highway, because drivers thought loaders checked the straps and loaders thought drivers did. He let things cool off and raised it at the quarterly meeting. By then people shrugged it off as a one-time slip. This morning a driver radios in to say another load has shifted.
examples.whatToDo: Gather drivers and loaders before the trucks leave today, and name one person who checks every strap before each truck pulls out.
examples.whyItMatters: A month of calm let the old not-my-job habit settle back in. The fresh scare is when people will accept a change.

examples.title: Exam week and a lost group grade
examples.scenario: Hyun-woo's college study group has no one in charge of handing in their shared report. Each person had assumed someone else would upload the final version. This week nobody did, and the group lost a tenth of its grade. He wants to fix it now. Clémence, who is stressed about her exams, snaps that they can sort it out next term.
examples.whatToDo: Tell Clémence she has a point about stress, then ask for five minutes today to choose who uploads every final version.
examples.whyItMatters: Next term the sting will be gone, and the group will slip back into hoping someone else does it.

questions.prompt: Your community theater's opening night goes dark when old stage wiring fails, wiring the crew had grumbled about for months. The cast is shaken. What do you do the next morning?
choices: Let everyone rest this week, then bring up the wiring at next month's meeting.
Track down the electrician who did the old wiring and ask them to cover the repairs.
Call cast and crew in today and agree who checks the wiring before each show.
questions.explanation: Today the dark stage is fresh in everyone's mind, so the crew will agree to a new wiring check. Waiting a month lets the old habit of grumbling and ignoring it settle back in.

questions.prompt: After a child goes missing at school pickup for an hour, the principal emails parents an apology. A full review of pickup, the email says, will start next term, once things settle. What is the trap in this plan?
choices: Expecting next term's review to work as well as one started this week.
Expecting an emailed apology to do as much as talking to parents in person.
Expecting one review to fix pickup without naming who was on duty.
questions.explanation: This week, staff and parents are shaken enough to accept new pickup rules. By next term the old way will feel normal again. The apology email is fine; the delay is the problem.

questions.prompt: A food truck's fryer catches fire because grease built up in a trap each cook thought someone else cleaned. The owner replaces the fryer and plans to sort out cleaning duties after the summer rush. What will most likely happen by autumn?
choices: The scare keeps everyone careful, so the grease trap gets cleaned anyway.
By autumn the old habit is back, and nobody cleans the grease trap.
The cooks spend the whole summer arguing over whose job the grease trap was.
questions.explanation: The fire loosened the crew's habits only for a short while. Waiting for the rush to end lets them set again, so the grease trap stays nobody's job. Being scared doesn't change who cleans it.

questions.prompt: Your friend coaches a kids' baseball team. On Saturday a player scraped a knee, and the first-aid kit was empty again. She plans to settle who restocks it at season's end, once the parents cool off. What's your best reply?
choices: "Get a bigger kit with double the supplies, so it lasts the whole season."
"Restock the kit yourself tonight so it's full for the next game."
"Set a restocking schedule with the parents this week, while they still care."
questions.explanation: The parents are paying attention now, so they'll agree to a restocking schedule this week. Restocking it yourself fixes the next game but leaves the gap that keeps emptying the kit.

questions.prompt: A library's outdoor book drop jams in a storm and ruins a bin of returns. Staff had worked around the faulty latch for a year. The head librarian rewrites the closing checklist that week, and staff follow it without a grumble. Why did the change go so smoothly?
choices: The staff had long wanted a clear checklist to follow.
The ruined books had shaken loose habits that usually resist change.
The head librarian had the power to order any checklist she liked.
questions.explanation: The ruined returns had everyone's attention, so the staff's settled habits were loose for a short while. The head librarian had that power all year; the change stuck because it came right after the storm.

questions.prompt: You manage a small dental office. A patient missed a crown fitting after a reminder mix-up, the third this year from the paper diary the front desk has hated for years. The staff are upset. What's your move this week?
choices: Move bookings off the paper diary this week, while the staff are fired up.
Ask the front desk to double-check the diary before each reminder goes out.
Book a calm review of the diary for next month, once everyone has settled down.
questions.explanation: The missed fitting has everyone ready to drop the diary they've put up with for years. Double-checking adds work to the same old diary, so the mix-ups keep coming.

questions.prompt: Two partners run an online shop. Each assumed the other was backing up the orders, until a server crash wiped a whole day of them. That week they rebuilt the shop's website and called it fixed. A month later, another day of orders vanished. Where did they slip up?
choices: Fixing it themselves instead of bringing in an outside tech expert.
Spending the crash week on the website, not the backups nobody owned.
Not warning their customers right away that more of their orders might vanish.
questions.explanation: The crash had them ready to change the backup routine each had left to the other. They spent that week on the website instead, so the same gap stayed open and orders vanished again.

reviewCards.front: Your choir's sheet music goes missing the night before a concert. Nobody was ever in charge of the music folder, and everyone is rattled. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Ask the choir that same week who keeps the folder from now on. People will agree while the scare still stings.

reviewCards.back: A group's habits are stuck most of the time. A crisis loosens them for a short while, and once things calm down they set again.

reviewCards.front: When something breaks and everyone says to sort it out once things cool off, the better plan is to ...
reviewCards.back: ... change the routine behind the problem that same week, while people still care enough to agree.

reviewCards.front: A bike shop's repair tags kept getting mixed up. After a customer's bike was sold by mistake, the owner apologized and planned a staff talk for next season. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The owner let the shock pass. The staff were ready to change the tagging habit that week, but by next season the mix-ups felt normal again.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what do you do the next time something goes badly wrong in a group you belong to?
reviewCards.back: Don't wait for calm. Change the routine everyone has been putting up with that week, because the chance closes once things settle.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting the short window after a setback when people will accept change, and acting inside it.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking we'll deal with it once things calm down, I name the routine behind the problem and suggest one change that same day.
When I sit down to the first meeting after something went wrong, I bring up one routine everyone has put up with and ask to change it that week.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, think of the last thing that went wrong at home or at work. Write down the routine behind it that everyone shrugs off.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, read your list of things you put up with. If one caused trouble that week, raise it within a day and ask to change it while people still care.

chapters.title: Why People Turn Down Good New Things
chapters.hook: Call your idea brand new and exciting, and people will slide it right back across the table, even when it's better than what they have.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a good new thing wins people over the moment they see it. Actually, people push new things away even when they like them, because the unfamiliar makes them uneasy until it sits beside something they already know.
chapters.keyTakeaway: To get someone to try something new, tuck it between things they already know and like.
chapters.tryThisNow: Tell one person today about something new you'd like them to try, opening with a thing they already love.

memorableLines.text: New things win people over when they arrive dressed as old friends.

breakdown.fastRead:
On Monday, Zainab's hardware store swaps its paper order book for a tablet. Her plan is a slideshow on how different it is. Her staff have used that book for years and eye the tablet like a stranger. If they shrug, the system she paid for gathers dust.

Charles Duhigg explains why that pitch backfires. People turn away from the unfamiliar, even things they would like. At Target, the store chain, numbers expert Andrew Pole could tell from what shoppers bought who was pregnant. Many of them felt spied on by the baby ads Target mailed. One father near Minneapolis complained about baby coupons sent to his teenage daughter, then apologized when he learned she was pregnant. So Target tucked the baby ads between lawn mowers and wineglasses, and the ads began working. Radio stations did the same for OutKast's Hey Ya!, which many listeners switched off at first. Played again and again between familiar songs, it became a huge hit.

So Zainab skips the slideshow. She sets the tablet beside the paper book and copies the book's columns onto the order screen. Everyone enters the Monday order there, over the usual coffee. She does the same every week. Once you tuck something new between things people already know and like, you find them trying it instead of turning it down.
