It sounded unlike anything they were used to. So stations began playing it between songs everyone already knew, again and again. Each time it came on, it felt a little less strange. In time it felt familiar, and it became a huge hit.

Food follows the same pattern. During World War II, the US government wanted families to eat organ meats such as liver and kidneys. Offered as strange new foods, they went uneaten. People did eat them once the meats were cooked into dishes they already made at home. The meat was the same. The meal around it was familiar.

You can use this at work or at home. Start with what the other person already knows and likes. Then set the new thing right between those pieces, in the usual place, at the usual time. Don't make the new thing stand out; hide it among familiar things, the way Target hid its baby coupons among lawn mowers and wineglasses. Don't sell how new it is. And give it more than one round, because a single try is seldom enough for something to stop feeling strange.

So Zainab skips the slideshow. She sets the tablet beside the paper book and copies the book's columns onto the order screen. On Monday, everyone enters the usual order together, over the usual coffee, and she does the same every week after. The tablet itself hasn't changed. Only what surrounds it is old and liked, and that is what lets her staff pick it up. Once you tuck something new between things people already know and like, you find them trying it instead of turning it down.

examples.title: A new cheese at the Saturday stall
examples.scenario: Oksana sells cheese from a folding table at a Saturday farmers' market. Her regulars buy the same mild cheddar every week. This month she has made a smoked goat cheese she is proud of, and it cost her two weeks of work. She has a chalkboard that could say NEW in big letters. Now she must decide where the goat cheese goes.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the NEW sign. Put small cubes of the goat cheese on the tasting board, between the cheddar and the brie regulars already reach for.
examples.whyItMatters: Next to cheeses they trust, the new one tastes like part of the usual order instead of a gamble.

examples.title: Dad's step counter stays in the drawer
examples.scenario: Hana's father was told by his doctor to walk more. She bought him a step-counting watch and spent an evening walking him through every feature and daily goal. Each morning he still walks only to the corner shop for his paper, cricket playing on his pocket radio. Three weeks on, the watch sits boxed in a drawer, and he changes the subject when she asks.
examples.whatToDo: Ask him to wear the watch on his usual paper run, and walk the long way round with him while the cricket plays.
examples.whyItMatters: The watch becomes part of a morning he already loves, so the extra steps feel like his routine, not a doctor's order.

examples.title: The band's first song falls flat
examples.scenario: Kofi, fifteen, plays bass in his school's lunchtime band and has written the band's first song of its own. Last week at rehearsal he slipped it in between the two covers everyone loves. The band played it once, shrugged, and went back to the covers. His face burned, and now he wants to drop the song before anyone calls it bad.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the song in that same spot, between the two favorite covers, at every rehearsal this month instead of dropping it.
examples.whyItMatters: One play is too few. Heard again and again beside songs they love, it starts to feel like one of theirs.

questions.prompt: A café owner adds an oat-milk drink and props a bright sign by the door saying it's brand new and like nothing else on the menu. Few customers order it. What was the trap?
choices: Selling it as unlike anything the regulars already drink and enjoy.
Hanging its sign by the door, not the counter.
Launching it before a tasting day showed whether customers liked the flavor.
questions.explanation: Calling the drink unlike anything on the menu makes it a stranger, so regulars stick with their usual. A tasting day would not fix that, since people can like something new and still turn it down.

questions.prompt: A library wants more people to borrow its new e-reader tablets. Staff move them from a glass case to the bestseller table, each loaded with that week's popular novels. What most likely happens?
choices: Borrowers overlook the tablets and keep taking home the paper copies.
Borrowers feel the library is pushing gadgets on them and complain at the desk.
More borrowers try a tablet, now that it sits among books they want.
questions.explanation: On the bestseller table, the tablets sit among books borrowers already want, so trying one feels like part of the usual visit. Nothing is being aimed at anyone, so there is little reason to feel spied on.

questions.prompt: Your friend runs a hair salon and is excited about a new scalp treatment. She says, "It's so good, I'll just add it to the top of the price board." What's your best reply?
choices: "Wait for the holiday rush, when more clients come in."
"Add a few minutes of it to the wash they already book."
"Put a card by the price board that lists every benefit it brings."
questions.explanation: Folding a few minutes into the wash clients already book lets them meet the treatment inside a visit they like. A busier season brings more people, but they would still meet it as a stranger on a list.

questions.prompt: A podcast host's new local history segment used to open the show, and many listeners skipped it. Mid-show, between two ad breaks, it was skipped too. Now it runs between the two segments fans love most, and they stay through it. Why does this work?
choices: In the middle, fans are too settled in to press skip.
Heard between parts they love, it now feels like one of them.
Fans can tell the host has put more care into the new segment.
questions.explanation: Between two segments fans already enjoy, the history piece starts to feel like part of the show they know. Mid-show between ad breaks, fans skipped it all the same, so being in the middle is not what holds them. Only its spot changed, so more care from the host cannot explain why they stay.

questions.prompt: You run a small office and want everyone to plan their week in a shared online calendar instead of on the old whiteboard. The Monday team lunch, a favorite, is coming up. What do you do?
choices: Pull up the calendar at Monday's lunch, filled in with the whiteboard's plans.
Hang a big poster that announces the calendar as a fresh start.
Send a step-by-step email first, so everyone learns each feature before the Monday lunch.
questions.explanation: Showing the calendar at a lunch the team likes, already holding the plans from their whiteboard, makes it look like the week they know. A fresh-start poster sells how new it is, which is what makes people pull back.

questions.prompt: A florist adds a dried-flower wreath to her shop. She hangs one among the rose bouquets on a Saturday, sells none, and takes it off the wall for good. What was her mistake?
choices: Showing it among bouquets instead of on a stand of its own.
Pricing the wreath higher than the bouquets shoppers already buy.
Giving up after one day, before the wreath could feel familiar.
questions.explanation: Among the bouquets was the right spot, but one Saturday is too short for something new to stop feeling strange. A stand of its own would only make the wreath stand out as new.

questions.prompt: A coach wants his kids' volleyball team to run a new passing drill. He slips it into warm-up between the two games the kids beg for, and keeps it there all month. What will the end of the month most likely look like?
choices: The kids run the drill as just another part of warm-up.
The kids rush through the drill to reach the games.
The kids tire of both games now the drill sits between them.
questions.explanation: A month of meeting the drill between two games they love lets it feel like part of practice, so they stop treating it as an extra. The games stay the same, so there is no reason they would sour.

reviewCards.front: Why do people often turn down a new thing even when they would enjoy it?
reviewCards.back: Because it feels strange, and strange feels risky. Set beside things they already know and like, it starts to feel like part of their usual life.

reviewCards.front: When your new idea keeps getting turned down, instead of explaining it harder, put it ...
reviewCards.back: ... right between things the other person already knows and likes, and keep it there until it stops feeling new.

reviewCards.front: A bike shop owner parked a new electric bike alone in the window under a big NEW sign. A month later, nobody had asked about it. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He showed it off as a stranger. Parked between the bikes his regulars already ride and trust, it would have looked like a next step, not a leap.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, how do you get someone to try something new?
reviewCards.back: Don't sell how new it is. Set it in among things they already know and enjoy, and give it time to feel familiar.

reviewCards.front: Your book club reads only thrillers, and you'd like the members to try a graphic novel.
reviewCards.back: Choose a graphic novel that's a thriller, and slot it between two of the club's usual picks.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Bringing people to new things by placing them inside what they already trust and enjoy.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself pitching something as brand new and different, I start again by naming something they already like and setting the new thing beside it.
When I finish writing my grocery list for the week, I plan one new food inside a meal my household already loves.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the end of today, pick one new thing you want someone to try. Write down two things they already enjoy that you could set it between.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: All week, bring the new thing back in that same spot, between the same two things the person likes. Note the day they first reach for it without being asked.

chapters.title: Why Change Spreads Through People You Barely Know
chapters.hook: Your garden-tool sharing plan stopped at the two friends who said yes. The neighbor you chat with at the recycling bins knows the whole street.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels natural to ask only your closest friends when you want people to join something. But a change spreads through people who know you a little, because they reach circles your friends never touch, and they feel the pull to join.
chapters.keyTakeaway: To spread a change past your own circle, recruit acquaintances, not just close friends.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one line naming three people you know only a little who could join what you're starting, and tape it to your bathroom mirror tonight.

memorableLines.text: Friends will come when you call. Acquaintances carry the call to everyone else.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why did one woman's arrest empty a city's buses when earlier arrests had not? In 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her seat on a bus. Other riders had been arrested on those buses before, and the city stayed quiet.

Charles Duhigg finds the answer in who knew her. Parks had close friends across the city's groups. Sociologists call bonds like these strong ties, and her friends rallied to her first. Then a boycott spread along weak ties, people who knew each other a little. Acquaintances reach circles your friends never touch. Sociologist Mark Granovetter found the same in job hunting: people got work more often through acquaintances than close friends. They also feel the group's pull. In Montgomery, riding the bus meant letting your neighbors down.

Most of us think our best friends are our best bet. They do say yes. But they mostly know the same people we do, so the word goes round one circle and stops. Parks's friends got the protest started, and people who barely knew her made it citywide. Stop asking only your closest friends, and start asking the people you know a little.
breakdown.deepRead:
Why did one woman's arrest empty a city's buses when earlier arrests had not? In 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her seat on a bus. Other riders had been arrested on those buses before, and the city stayed quiet. Her arrest set off a boycott across the whole city.

Charles Duhigg finds the answer in who knew her. Parks was well liked, with close friends across the city's many groups, rich and poor. Sociologists call bonds like these strong ties. When she was jailed, those friends rallied first. One bailed her out, and others started urging people to stay off the buses. Friends alone, though, make a small protest. The boycott spread along weak ties, people who knew each other only a little, from church or down the street. Pastors told their congregations, and neighbors told neighbors. Acquaintances also feel the pull of the group. In Montgomery, riding the bus during the boycott meant letting down people who would notice. The boycott lasted, Duhigg says, because a leader gave people new habits and a new sense of who they were, so it could carry on by itself.

Most of us think our best friends are our best bet, and that people who barely know us won't care. Friends do say yes. But close friends tend to know the same people we do, so the word goes round one circle and stops. Acquaintances reach circles your friends never touch. A sociologist, Mark Granovetter, saw this in job hunting. People landed jobs more often through acquaintances than through close friends. The acquaintances heard about openings the friends never did.

Your own plans work the same way. Say you want your street to share one set of garden tools. Your two closest friends there say yes at once. The neighbor you chat with at the recycling bins knows the families at the far end. Parks's friends got the protest started, and people who barely knew her made it citywide. Stop asking only your closest friends, and start asking the people you know a little.
breakdown.fullRead:
Why did one woman's arrest empty a city's buses when earlier arrests had not? In 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her seat on a bus. Other riders had been arrested on those buses before, and the city stayed quiet. Her arrest set off a boycott across the whole city.

Charles Duhigg finds the answer in who knew her. Parks was well liked and belonged to many of the city's groups. Her close friends came from across Montgomery, rich and poor. Sociologists call bonds like these strong ties, the kind between people who know each other well. When she was jailed, those friends rallied first. One bailed her out, and others started urging people to stay off the buses.

Friends alone, though, make a small protest. The boycott spread along weak ties, people who knew each other only a little, from church or down the street. Pastors told their congregations. Neighbors told neighbors. And acquaintances feel a pull that strangers do not. They see each other at church, at the store, on the walk home. In Montgomery, riding the bus during the boycott meant letting down people who would notice. Sitting out the protest was no longer a private choice. The boycott lasted, Duhigg says, because a leader gave people new habits and a new sense of who they were, so it could carry on by itself.

A sociologist, Mark Granovetter, found the same reach in job hunting. People landed new jobs more often through acquaintances than through close friends. That sounds backward, since friends care about you more. But your friends tend to know the same people you do and hear the same news. Acquaintances move in other circles, so they hear about openings your friends never do.

Another study looked at people who signed up to spend a summer in Mississippi registering Black voters. Not all of them went. The ones who did tended to belong to church and community groups, where many people knew they had signed up. Backing out would have meant facing all of those people. The ties that kept them going were not only close friendships. They were the wider web of people who knew them a little.

Most of us think our best friends are our best bet, and that people who barely know us won't care. Friends do say yes, and they say it quickly. That quick yes is what fools us. Because close friends know the same people we do, the word goes round one circle and stops. A plan can look healthy for weeks while it never reaches one new face.

Your own plans work the same way. Say you want your street to share one set of garden tools. Your two closest friends on the street say yes on the spot. Then it stalls, since they know the same few houses you do. The neighbor you chat with at the recycling bins knows the families at the far end. The man who runs the corner shop knows half the block. Ask them, and ask where others can see, and the street hears about it.

So the puzzle has a plain answer. Parks's friends got the protest started, and people who barely knew her made it citywide. Stop asking only your closest friends, and start asking the people you know a little.

examples.title: A chess club that won't grow
examples.scenario: Dmitri plays chess in the park every Sunday with his two oldest friends. He wants a real club, with a dozen boards going under the oak trees. Both friends said yes the moment he asked. Now his phone is in his hand, his contacts list open, and he has to choose who gets the next message.
examples.whatToDo: Message the people he knows a little instead: the barista who plays online, the neighbor with a chess set, the coworker who brought it up.
examples.whyItMatters: Each of them knows players Dmitri has never met, so the club can grow past his own small circle.

examples.title: Exam sessions nobody else joined
examples.scenario: Aiyana, an apprentice electrician, set up Thursday evening study sessions for the licensing exam. She asked her two best friends on her crew, and they came every week. After a month it was still the three of them, and the training center gave their room to a bigger group. Her friends shrug and say nobody else cares.
examples.whatToDo: At the next morning safety talk, invite by name the apprentices she only nods to, starting with those from other crews.
examples.whyItMatters: Apprentices on other crews know people her friends never work with, and a session others attend is harder to skip.

examples.title: Fifty signatures before five
examples.scenario: The council will pave over the nursery's vegetable garden unless fifty families sign a letter by five o'clock today. Kwame, who teaches the toddler room, has signed with the four colleagues he eats lunch with. It is half past two, and pickup starts at three. If the letter falls short, the children lose the beds they planted in spring.
examples.whatToDo: At the gate during pickup, hand the letter to parents he only greets by name, and ask each to post it in their own group chat.
examples.whyItMatters: In half an hour he cannot reach fifty families himself, but parents he barely knows can each reach many more.

questions.prompt: A cyclist wants a weekly Saturday group ride from the town square. He invites only his three closest cycling friends. What most likely happens next?
choices: His friends bring in others quickly, since close friends try hardest.
His friends turn up, and the ride stays those same four people.
His friends turn up, and others join after seeing the group ride past.
questions.explanation: Close friends mostly know the same people he does, so the invite goes round one small circle and stops. Riders who spot the group in passing were never asked and have no tie pulling them in.

questions.prompt: A coworker says, "My closest friends at work signed up for my step challenge, but everyone else here barely knows me. Why would they care?" What's your best reply?
choices: Try the people you chat with at the coffee machine, since they know other teams.
Explain the health benefits more clearly, so everyone sees why it matters to them.
Send the whole office a survey first, to learn what kind of challenge people would enjoy.
questions.explanation: People you chat with at the coffee machine know whole teams your friends never talk to, so the challenge can travel. A survey only delays asking, and still leaves the people you half know out.

questions.prompt: A new parent started a weekend toy swap. Her close friends came first. Then she mentioned it to parents she half knew from swim lessons, and forty families came. Why did it spread so far?
choices: Parents she half knew were more polite and less likely to say no.
The swim parents had more free weekends than her close friends.
Each of those parents knew families her own friends had never met.
questions.explanation: The swim parents reached families in circles her friends never touch, so word got to new homes. Politeness would not explain it, since being polite only gets a yes from the person you ask.

questions.prompt: Your two closest friends have agreed to help you run a free clothes-mending evening at the community hall. You have one week to fill the room. What do you do?
choices: Ask the people from your dance class and street whom you half know.
Promise a prize draw to everyone who brings a torn shirt along.
Post it on the town's online notice board, where many strangers might see it.
questions.explanation: People from your dance class and street know you a little and reach circles your two friends never touch. Strangers scrolling a notice board have no tie to you, so nothing pulls them in.

questions.prompt: A nurse wants the night shift to use a new handover checklist. She asks her two closest friends on the ward to try it, and they use it every shift. Months later, only those three use it. What went wrong for her?
choices: She made the checklist too long for a rushed handover.
She counted on two close friends to carry it to everyone.
She never offered staff a small reward for using it each shift.
questions.explanation: Her two friends work alongside the same people she does, so the checklist went round one small circle and stopped. A reward would not have fixed that, because the rest of the night shift was never asked.

questions.prompt: A gardener asks members of his allotment group, people he knows a little, to stop buying from a seed seller who overcharges. At the monthly meeting, run by the group's chair, several agree in front of everyone. What is the likely result?
choices: Most of the members stay out, since they barely know him.
They wait to see whether the group's chair backs it before they decide.
More members join, since staying out now feels like letting others down.
questions.explanation: Members who know him a little watched others agree at the meeting, so staying out now means letting the group down. Waiting on the chair misses that the pull comes from fellow members.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'm starting a free film night at the community center. I won't bother my close friends. I'll only ask people I barely know, since they spread things further." What do you say back?
choices: Good plan, since close friends would only keep it inside one circle.
Get your close friends on board first, then ask people you half know.
Post it online instead, since strangers reach even further than people you half know.
questions.explanation: Close friends are the ones who show up first and get a new thing going. People you half know then carry it into other circles. Skip the friends and nobody is there to start it.

reviewCards.front: Your close friends have already said yes to your plan. To get it beyond them, the next people to ask are ...
reviewCards.back: ... the people you know only a little, from your class, your street or your job, because they know whole circles your friends never meet.

reviewCards.front: A man started a weekly park run with his four best mates and asked nobody else. A year later it is still those five. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: His mates know mostly the same people he does, so the invite went round one circle and stopped. Asking runners he only half knew would have carried it further.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, how do you get a new idea to travel beyond your own friends?
reviewCards.back: Let close friends get it started, then ask the people you half know, since they reach circles your friends never touch.

reviewCards.front: You want neighbors in your apartment block to share one weekly grocery run. Your closest friend in the block is already in. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Ask the neighbors you only chat with in the lift, and ask where others can see, like the block's group chat, so joining feels expected.

reviewCards.front: Why do people who barely know you often carry news further than your closest friends?
reviewCards.back: Your close friends tend to know the same people you do. Acquaintances belong to other circles, so the news reaches homes your friends never would.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Carrying a new idea beyond your inner circle by asking the people you half know.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I arrive at a club or group I go to each week, I tell one person there I only know by face what I'm starting, and ask them to come.
When I catch myself thinking they barely know me, so why care, I ask that person anyway, and tell them who has already said yes.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, send one message about something you care about to a person you know only a little, such as a neighbor or a classmate, and invite them in.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, once your friends have heard about your plan, ask two people from a group you belong to but don't know well. Note who they bring along.

chapters.title: Once You Can See a Habit, Changing It Is Yours
chapters.hook: Once you can point to the desk drawer where your afternoon chocolate waits, that habit stops happening to you. You're choosing it.
chapters.counterintuition: You have probably been told that some habits are just how you're wired, so they aren't really your fault. The trouble is that once you can see a habit's cue and reward, you can pick a different routine, so changing it is your job.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Once you can name a habit's cue, routine and reward, changing it becomes your job.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before dinner, write down one habit you call just how you are, and beside it the one change you'll make.

memorableLines.text: A habit you can describe is no longer something you can blame on wiring.

breakdown.fastRead:
Knowing how a habit works doesn't let you off the hook. It puts you on it. Charles Duhigg shows why. Angie Bachmann, a stay-at-home mother, gambled away her inheritance and her house. When the casino company chased her for debts, she sued back, saying it had used her habit against her. She lost. Brian Thomas killed his wife in his sleep, thinking he was fighting off an attacker. He was unaware of it and was not held to blame. The man asleep could not see his habit. Bachmann knew about hers and could have chosen to change it, so Duhigg holds her responsible.

Habits feel like wiring because they run before you think. Yet each has three parts you can name: the cue that sets it off, the routine you do and the reward you get. Once you can name them, you have a choice.

So test any habit you call just how you are. Say it's the afternoon chocolate from your desk drawer. The cue is the three o'clock slump, the routine is opening the drawer, and the reward is a break. Name all three, and the excuse is gone. Pick one change and start it today. Whoever can name a habit's cue, routine and reward is in charge of changing it.
breakdown.deepRead:
Knowing how a habit works doesn't let you off the hook. It puts you on it. Charles Duhigg shows why with two people whose habits did terrible harm. Angie Bachmann was a stay-at-home mother who began visiting a casino to break up long, empty days. Her gambling grew. Then her parents died and left her money. The casino company courted her with free trips, and she gambled away her inheritance and her house. When the company chased her for unpaid debts, she sued back, saying it had used her habit against her. She lost.

Brian Thomas had walked in his sleep for years. One night he killed his wife while asleep, thinking he was fighting off an attacker. He had no awareness of what his brain was doing, and he was not held to blame. Duhigg sets the two cases side by side. In both, a pattern was running on its own. The difference was seeing. The man asleep could not see his habit. Bachmann knew about hers and could have chosen to change it, so Duhigg holds her responsible. Habits, he argues, are not destiny.

Most of us feel more like the sleeper than we really are. A habit runs before you think, so it feels like wiring rather than a choice. You don't decide to reach for the snack or the phone. It just happens. Yet every habit has three parts you can learn to name. There's the cue that sets it off, the routine you do, and the reward you get. Once you can name them, you have a choice. A company may play on your habit, as the casino did, but that doesn't take the choice from you.

So test any habit you call just how you are. Say it's the afternoon chocolate from your desk drawer. The cue is the three o'clock slump. The routine is opening the drawer. The reward is a break. Name all three, and the excuse is gone. Duhigg leans on the philosopher William James here, who held that believing you can change is part of what makes change happen. So pick one change, such as a lap of the stairwell for your break, and start it today. Whoever can name a habit's cue, routine and reward is in charge of changing it.
breakdown.fullRead:
Knowing how a habit works doesn't let you off the hook. It puts you on it. Charles Duhigg shows why with two people whose habits did terrible harm. One was held responsible and lost everything. The other walked free. What separates them is the whole point.

Angie Bachmann was a stay-at-home mother. Once her children were in school, her days felt long and empty, and she began visiting a casino for a break. At first she set herself limits on time and money. Over time the visits grew longer, the bets grew bigger, and the limits slipped.

Then her parents died and left her money. The casino company took notice. It courted her with free trips and other perks, and she gambled more than ever. In the end she lost her inheritance and her house. When the company chased her for unpaid debts, she sued back. She said it had known about her habit and used it against her. She lost.

Brian Thomas had walked in his sleep for years. One night, while asleep, he killed his wife, thinking he was fighting off an attacker. He had no awareness of what his brain was doing. He was not held to blame.

Duhigg sets the two cases side by side. In both, a pattern ran on its own and did terrible harm. The difference was seeing. The man asleep could not see his habit. Bachmann knew about her gambling and could have chosen to change it. So Duhigg holds her responsible, even though the casino played on her habit. Habits, he argues, are not destiny. Once you know one is there, changing it is your job.

Most of us feel more like the sleeper than we really are. A habit runs before you think, so it feels like wiring rather than a choice. You don't decide to reach for the snack or the phone. It just happens. Yet every habit has three parts you can learn to name. There's the cue that sets it off, the routine you do, and the reward you get. Once you can name them, you have a choice. A company may play on your habit, as the casino did. That doesn't take the choice from you.

Duhigg also turns to the philosopher William James, who held that believing you can change is what makes change possible. Calling a habit your wiring is a quiet bet that it can't move. Naming its parts, and believing you can act on them, gives you somewhere to start.

So test any habit you call just how you are. Say it's the afternoon chocolate from your desk drawer. The cue is the three o'clock slump. The routine is opening the drawer. The reward is a break. Name all three, and the excuse is gone. Then pick one change, such as a lap of the stairwell for your break, and start it today. Whoever can name a habit's cue, routine and reward is in charge of changing it.

examples.title: A sharp reply to the biggest client
examples.scenario: Osei sells office furniture, and after every tense call with his biggest client, he fires off a sharp email. He has always blamed his temper. This week he finally saw the pattern: the client complains, he types fast, and he gets the thrill of having the last word. Now a new complaint sits in his inbox. His reply is written, and the cursor rests on Send.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the sharp reply as his to change, save it as a draft, and call the client after lunch instead.
examples.whyItMatters: He can name the complaint, the typing and the thrill, so his temper is no excuse, and his biggest client is at stake.

examples.title: Six extra driving lessons, same hard brake
examples.scenario: Ingrid's driving instructor keeps flagging the same thing: whenever a truck pulls up close behind her, she brakes hard. She told him she's just a nervous driver and booked six extra lessons, hoping it would wear off. Six paid lessons later, she still brakes hard. Last lesson she named the parts herself: truck in the mirror, foot on the brake, a flash of safety. Her test is in two weeks.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the nervous-driver label, tell her instructor the braking is hers to fix, and plan what her foot does when a truck appears.
examples.whyItMatters: The extra lessons were waiting for the habit to fade. Now that she can name its parts, changing it is up to her.

examples.title: The phone at his mother's birthday lunch
examples.scenario: At his mother's birthday lunch, Rohan's sister says, in front of everyone, that he grabs his phone whenever their mother starts an old story. His mother goes quiet, and his face burns. He knows the pattern: the story begins, he reaches for the phone, and he gets a break from the boredom. Everything in him wants to say that phones are built to hook people.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the line about phones, tell his mother his sister is right, put the phone in his coat, and ask her to finish the story.
examples.whyItMatters: He already sees the story, the reach and the break, so blaming the phone would only guard his pride while his mother pays.

questions.prompt: A coworker tells you, "Every day at noon I eat at my desk and scroll my phone. The afternoon slump hits, and scrolling is an easy break. That's just me." What is your best reply?
choices: "Then go easy on yourself, since lots of people are built that way."
"Get a teammate to drag you out at noon, since you won't go alone."
"You've named the slump and the break, so changing noon is up to you."
questions.explanation: Your coworker can already name the slump, the scrolling and the easy break, so it isn't wiring anymore, and changing it is theirs to do. Going easy treats as fixed a habit they can now see. Getting a teammate to drag them out leaves the habit in someone else's hands and agrees they can't change it themselves.

questions.prompt: A cashier always said she was just a nail-biter. Last month she noticed she bites when the line gets long, and the biting calms her. Since then she has stopped calling it who she is, and she presses her thumbs together when the line grows. The biting is fading. What made the difference?
choices: Fighting the urge hard every day finally wore it down for good.
Seeing what set it off and what it gave her let her choose.
Dropping the excuse made her feel guilty enough to finally quit biting her nails.
questions.explanation: Once she could name the long line, the biting and the calm it gave her, she had a choice. Guilt wasn't what changed. She started choosing a different move whenever the line grew.

questions.prompt: For months you've snapped at your partner within a minute of getting home from late shifts. On the drive home tonight it clicks: you walk in drained, you snap, and letting off steam feels good. What do you do?
choices: Own the snapping as yours to fix, and plan your first minute inside tonight.
Wait for a calm weekend, when you'll have the time to think it all through.
Decide the job is the real cause, and ask for fewer late shifts.
questions.explanation: You can name the cue, the snapping and the relief, so it's yours to change from tonight. Waiting for a calm weekend means your partner meets the same snap at the door again.

questions.prompt: A friend bets on football every Sunday as the games kick off. He knows the pattern: kickoff, the bet, the buzz. Now he's furious that his betting app keeps sending free-bet offers, and he says the app is the real problem. What is the trap in his thinking?
choices: Thinking he has to learn more about why he bets before acting.
Thinking he has to give up watching football before the Sunday betting can stop.
Thinking the app's offers make the betting its fault, not his to fix.
questions.explanation: He can already name kickoff, the bet and the buzz, so changing it is his job, whatever the app sends. He doesn't need to study it more first. He knows enough to start.

questions.prompt: During a busy term, a teacher can describe his after-school habit exactly. After the last bell he sits down with his phone for one minute, the minute becomes forty, and it gives him quiet after a loud day. He shrugs and says he's just someone who needs to unwind. His marking piles up. What will most likely happen this month?
choices: The pile shrinks on its own once the busy part of term calms down.
He stops once the pile grows big enough to frighten him.
The forty minutes keep happening, since he still blames them on his nature.
questions.explanation: He can name the bell, the phone and the quiet, yet he files it under who he is, so the habit keeps running. A calmer term changes his workload, not the choice he hasn't made.

questions.prompt: You manage a sales team. One rep keeps skipping his call notes. He says he's not a details person, then explains: the call ends, he jumps straight to the next one, and the rush keeps him going. What do you say back?
choices: "You just told me exactly how it happens, so fixing it is on you."
"Then let's look for a role with less paperwork for you to do."
"Fair enough, some people just aren't built for the fiddly detail side of sales."
questions.explanation: He has just named the cue, the routine and the reward himself, so this is no longer about how he's built. A role with less paperwork only dodges a habit he already understands.

questions.prompt: For years a father called himself a shouter. Then he noticed the shouting comes at bath time, when he's tired and the kids splash, and it gets them out fast. He now calls the shouting his job to change, sets a two-minute timer for the kids to race, and the shouting has dropped off. Why is it fading?
choices: Admitting it out loud shamed him into keeping his voice down at night.
Calling it his job turned bath time into a choice he makes each night.
The kids grew older and calmer, so bath time gave him less to shout about.
questions.explanation: Once he could name the splashing, the tiredness and the quick result, calling it his job turned each bath time into a choice. Shame wasn't what changed. Choosing the timer over the shout was.

reviewCards.front: A woman could describe her evening habit exactly: the kids asleep, the glass of wine, the feeling the day is over. She kept saying she was just wired that way. A year later, nothing had changed. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She could see every part of the habit but still treated it as wiring. Once she could name what set it off and what it gave her, changing it was her job, and she never took it on.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what changes the moment you can name a habit's cue, routine and reward?
reviewCards.back: The habit stops being something that just happens to you. You can see how it works, so changing it is now your job.

reviewCards.front: You realise you open a news app every time a work task gets hard, and it gives you a small escape. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Stop calling it a quirk. You've named the hard task, the app and the escape, so pick one change for the next hard task and start it today.

reviewCards.front: Why can't someone who can describe a habit in detail still call it just how they're wired?
reviewCards.back: Because naming what sets it off, what they do and what they get gives them a choice. A habit they can choose about is theirs to change.

reviewCards.front: When a company plays on a habit you already understand, the job of changing it still belongs to ...
reviewCards.back: ... you, because you can see how the habit works, and no one else's tricks take that choice away.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Taking charge of a habit once you can see how it works, instead of blaming how you're built.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I get home from work each evening, I notice which habit kicks in first, name its cue, routine and reward, and choose one change for that evening.
When I hear myself say a habit is just how I am, I name its cue, routine and reward right there, and if I can, I pick one change and start it that day.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, catch the habit you wrote down just as its cue appears, and make your one change that time, even if only for a few minutes.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each week, look back at the habit you've taken on. Count the days you made your change, and set the next small step for the week ahead.
